files.lesson.md: --- order: 11 unit: brackets node: AC9M8A01 n2 title: Factorising summary: "Factorising is expanding backwards. Share the terms into equal rows: 6x + 9 is 3 rows of 2x + 3, so 3(2x + 3). Take out the highest common factor, then check by expanding." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "6 x-tiles and 9 ones. Can you share them into equal rows, with nothing left over?" connection: equal-rows # data/connections/maths.yml (Make on paper and Also used in; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8167 url: http://127.0.0.1:8167/index.html readySelector: "#sl-k" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: factor.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$6x + 9$ shared into 3 equal rows: each row is $2x + 3$, so $6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@factor.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Share the tiles into equal rows" say: "Factorising shares the tiles into equal rows." clip: - caption: { text: "6x + 9: 6 x-tiles and 9 ones.", say: "Six x tiles and nine ones." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "2 rows: 9 ones do not share into 2.", say: "Two rows do not work: nine ones do not share into two." } - click: Make k bigger - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "3 rows of 2x + 3: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).", say: "Three rows of two x plus three. That is the bracket." } - click: Make k bigger - expect: { selector: "#tsum", contains: "6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)" } - wait: 1200 --- In Expanding brackets you turned $3(2x + 4)$ into $6x + 12$. **Factorising** goes the other way: from $6x + 12$ back to a bracket. ## Predict: fully factorised ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a factorisation of 6x + 9 before using the board tests whether they divide every term, and whether they take out the biggest number." check: type: predict q: "Which is $6x + 9$ written as a bracket, with the biggest possible number outside?" options: - "$3(2x + 3)$" - "$6(x + 9)$" - "$3(2x + 9)$" - "$2(3x + 4.5)$" actual: "3(2x + 3). 3 goes into 6 and into 9: 6x ÷ 3 = 2x and 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Check by expanding: 3 × 2x = 6x and 3 × 3 = 9." ``` Can you share all the tiles into equal rows, with nothing left over? How many rows can you make at most? ## Run: share into rows ```step stage: run insight: "Trying k = 1, 2, 3 on the tiles shows which numbers of rows work (the ones that divide both totals) and what each row holds." try: { playground: board, starter: "factor.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "The board has $6x + 9$. Change $k$, the number of rows, until the tiles share into equal rows with more than one row. Was your prediction right?", when: "k = 3 and f = 1" } ``` $k$ is the number of rows. Factorising is sharing the tiles into equal rows: when they share equally, the board writes the bracket, with the number of rows ($k$) outside and one row inside. ## Investigate: the highest common factor ```step stage: investigate insight: "Factorising divides every term by a common factor; taking out the highest common factor leaves nothing more to share, and expanding checks it. Ava's mistake takes out a common factor that is not the highest." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Factorise $10x + 15$ fully." answer: "5(2x + 3)" form: factorised feedback: - ["5(2x + 15)", "Divide every term: 15 ÷ 5 = 3."] - ["5(5x + 10)", "Divide by 5, don't subtract it: 10x ÷ 5 = 2x."] explain: "The HCF of 10 and 15 is 5: 10x ÷ 5 = 2x and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Check: 5 × 2x + 5 × 3 = 10x + 15." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ava" text: "Ava factorises $12x - 8$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: hcf-not-highest explain: "Line 2: 2 goes into both, but 4 is the biggest. 6x − 4 still shares a 2, so it is not fully factorised: 12x − 8 = 4(3x − 2)." - check: type: question q: "How can you check that $4(3x - 2)$ is right for $12x - 8$?" options: ["Expand it and compare", "Add 4 to each term", "Check that 3 and 2 are both prime"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Factorising divides; the check multiplies back.", "That says nothing about 12x − 8."] explain: "Expand: 4 × 3x = 12x and 4 × (−2) = −8. You are back to 12x − 8." ``` ### Take out the HCF Here is how to factorise, then check. ```worked 12x - 8 :: Find a number that goes into every term. \text{HCF of } 12 \text{ and } 8 = 4 :: Take out the biggest: the highest common factor. 12x \div 4 = 3x :: Divide every term by 4. -8 \div 4 = -2 :: The sign comes too. 4(3x - 2) :: The HCF goes outside; what is left goes inside. 4 \times 3x - 4 \times 2 = 12x - 8 :: Check by expanding. ``` Try one: factorise $10x + 15$. ### Find the mistake Read Ava's working one line at a time. Is her answer wrong, or just not finished? ### Check it ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: different numbers on the board, a minus sign, three terms, a letter as the common factor, then the edge case of nothing to take out." try: { playground: board, starter: "factor.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - starter: "factor.yml#vary" hint: "Which numbers go into both 10 and 15? Try the biggest." check: { type: board, text: "The board has $10x + 15$. Share it into the most rows that work.", when: "h = 1", explain: "5 rows of 2x + 3: 10x + 15 = 5(2x + 3)." } - check: type: answer q: "Factorise $9x - 6$ fully." answer: "3(3x - 2)" form: factorised feedback: - ["3(3x + 2)", "The minus comes too: −6 ÷ 3 = −2."] - ["3(3x - 6)", "Divide every term: 6 ÷ 3 = 2."] explain: "HCF 3: 9x ÷ 3 = 3x and −6 ÷ 3 = −2. Check: 3(3x − 2) = 9x − 6." - check: type: answer q: "Three terms: factorise $4x + 8y - 12$ fully." answer: "4(x + 2y - 3)" form: factorised feedback: - ["4(x + 8y - 12)", "Divide every term by 4, not only the first."] - ["2(2x + 4y - 6)", "2 goes into all three, but 4 is bigger."] explain: "4 goes into 4, 8 and 12: 4(x + 2y − 3)." - check: type: answer q: "A letter can be a common factor too. Factorise $2x^2 + 4x$ fully." answer: "2x(x + 2)" form: factorised feedback: - ["2(x^2 + 2x)", "x goes into both terms as well: take it out too."] - ["x(2x + 4)", "2 goes into both terms as well."] explain: "2 and x go into both: 2x² ÷ 2x = x and 4x ÷ 2x = 2, so 2x(x + 2)." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: can $7x + 5$ be factorised?" options: ["No: no number bigger than 1 goes into 7 and 5", "Yes: 7(x + 5)", "Yes: 5(7x + 1)"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Expand it: 7(x + 5) = 7x + 35.", "Expand it: 5(7x + 1) = 35x + 5."] explain: "The HCF of 7 and 5 is 1, so 7x + 5 is already as simple as it gets. On the board, only 1 row works." ``` ### On the board Each task changes one thing. ### A minus sign No board from here: divide each term, then check by expanding. ### Three terms ### A letter in common ### Nothing to take out ## Practise: factorise and check ```step stage: practise insight: "Factorising with each sign and full working, mixed; stopping at a common factor that is not the highest is the planted slip, and the review keeps expanding fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Factorise $15x + 20$ fully." answer: "5(3x + 4)" form: factorised feedback: - ["5(3x + 20)", "Divide every term by 5."] explain: "HCF 5: 5(3x + 4)." - check: type: answer q: "Factorise $8x - 12$ fully." answer: "4(2x - 3)" form: factorised feedback: - ["2(4x - 6)", "4x − 6 still shares a 2. Take out the biggest: 4."] - ["4(2x + 3)", "The minus comes too: −12 ÷ 4 = −3."] explain: "HCF 4: 4(2x − 3)." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What's the biggest number that goes into both 8 and 12?", answer: 4, explain: "4: 8 = 4 × 2 and 12 = 4 × 3. That's the number outside the bracket." } - check: type: working q: "Factorise $18x + 12$ fully. You may take out a factor in steps. Write one step per line." start: "18x + 12" form: factorised example: ["2(9x + 6)", "6(3x + 2)"] wrong: [["2(9x + 6)"], ["6(3x + 12)"]] explain: "2(9x + 6) still shares a 3, so take it out too: 6(3x + 2). Or take out the HCF 6 straight away." - check: type: answer q: "Review: expand $3(2x - 5)$." answer: "6x - 15" form: expanded feedback: - ["6x - 5", "The 3 multiplies the 5 as well."] explain: "3 × 2x = 6x and 3 × (−5) = −15." ``` ### Positive ### A minus sign ### Full working ### Review: expanding ## Make: four rows ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing tiles that factorise fully with exactly 4 outside reverses the lesson: from the factor back to the expression." try: { playground: board, starter: "factor.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["Both numbers must be in the 4 times table.", "But the rows must not share further: 8 and 16 have HCF 8, not 4."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $s$ and $t$ so that $sx + t$ is fully factorised with 4 outside the bracket, then set $k$ to 4.", when: "k = 4 and h = 1", explain: "8x + 12 = 4(2x + 3), 4x + 8 = 4(x + 2) and 12x + 4 = 4(3x + 1) all work. 8x + 8 does not: its HCF is 8." } ``` Find an expression $sx + t$ that factorises fully as $4(\ldots)$. Then find another. Stretch: why can't $s$ and $t$ both be multiples of 8? ## Make: equal rows on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing the highest common factor decides how many equal rows there are; the paper task asks why the answer is 6 and not a smaller factor." hint: ["Find a number that goes into both 12 and 18.", "Then check that the rows cannot share more."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "You have 12 long tiles ($x$) and 18 small tiles (1). On paper, lay them in the greatest number of equal rows with none left over. Write the expression as a number of rows times one row, and check by expanding." steps: - ["$12x + 18$", "12 long tiles and 18 small ones"] - ["The highest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6", "the most equal rows is the highest common factor"] - ["$12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3)$", "divide both terms by 6"] - ["Check: $6 \\times 2x + 6 \\times 3 = 12x + 18$", "expanding gets back to the start"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why 6 rows?" options: - "6 is the highest common factor, so no more rows share equally" - "3 is the first common factor you find, so use that" - "30 is the sum of 12 and 18" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "3 rows work, but the bracket 4x + 6 still shares a 2. Take out the highest.", "Rows must divide both numbers evenly; adding them is not that."] answer: "6" answerLabel: "Rows" feedback: - ["3", "3 rows work, but the rows still share a factor of 2. Take out the highest common factor."] - ["2", "2 rows work, but 12 and 18 share a bigger factor. Look for the highest."] criteria: - "I used the highest common factor, not just any common factor." - "Each row is the same: 2x + 3." - "I checked by expanding." explain: "The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, so 12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3): 6 rows of 2 long tiles and 3 small ones." ``` Do this one in your book. The tile numbers are made up, but laying out tiles or chairs in equal rows is a real job. Write the factorised form and check it by expanding, then type the number of rows and choose the reason. **Also used in** - **Tiling and seating.** Laying tiles or chairs in equal rows with none left over is finding the highest common factor. - **Mental maths.** $7 \times 13 + 7 \times 7 = 7(13 + 7) = 140$. - **Next lessons.** Rearranging formulas, and factorising quadratics in Years 9 and 10. ```teacher summary: Students share algebra tiles into equal rows to factorise sx + t, learn to take out the highest common factor (numbers, then letters) and check by expanding (AC9M8A01, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can factorise an expression by taking out a common factor. - I can take out the highest common factor, including a letter, so the expression is fully factorised. - I can check a factorisation by expanding it. struggle: Stopping at a common factor that is not the highest, and finding a letter in common (2x² and 4x share a 2 and an x). Ask 'do the terms inside the bracket share anything?' and always check by expanding. before: > Do the Run board and the Make task yourself first. Students need Expanding brackets (the lesson before) and highest common factors from Year 7 Number. The one idea: factorising divides every term by a common factor, and the factor goes outside the bracket. The common mistake is taking out a common factor that is not the highest (12x − 8 = 2(6x − 4)); it is planted after the method, in Ava's working. Her answer is equal to 12x − 8, so it is not wrong, just not finished: that is the conversation to have. Answers are marked by form: an equal answer that could still be factorised further is told so ("could take out more") rather than marked right. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 6(x + 9) divided only the first term; those who chose 2(3x + 4.5) found a factor of 6 but not of 9. Do not correct it yet." - "Run: ask why 2 rows do not work (9 ones do not share into 2) and why 3 does." - "Investigate: model the worked example live, including the check by expanding. Then ask: is Ava's answer wrong?" - "Modify: before the letter task, ask what goes into both 2x² and 4x. Students often find the 2 and miss the x." - "Make: collect students' expressions on the board and ask which ones are fully factorised with 4 outside." - "Paper: equal rows is worked in books (HCF, factorised form, check by expanding). The page marks 6 and the reason it is 6 and not 3. Books out, then look at the page for the model." stuck: - see: A student divides only the first term (6x + 9 = 3(2x + 9)). ask: Expand your answer. Do you get back to where you started? fix: "Expanding is the check: 3 × 9 = 27, not 9." - see: A student stops at a common factor that is not the highest (Ava's mistake). ask: Look inside the bracket. Do those terms share anything? fix: "Take out what they share as well: 2(6x − 4) = 2 × 2(3x − 2) = 4(3x − 2)." - see: A student cannot find a common factor. ask: List the factors of each number. Which appear in both lists? fix: "Use the board: try k = 2, 3, 4… and see which numbers of rows work." stretch: "Factorise 6x²y − 9xy² fully. (3xy(2x − 3y).) Then: write three different expressions whose full factorisation has 6 outside." support: "Use the tiles board for every two-term question with positive numbers: try each k and read off the bracket." leads: > Next: rearranging formulas (node 3), which divides every term by a number in the same way. Where it leads: factorising quadratics in Years 9 and 10, which the same tiles show as a rectangle. exit: q: Factorise 14x − 21 fully, then check by expanding. a: "7(2x − 3). Check: 7 × 2x = 14x and 7 × (−3) = −21." explain: > **Factorising** is expanding backwards. Find a number that goes into every term, divide every term by it, and put it outside the bracket. $6x + 9$: 3 goes into 6 and 9, so $6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)$. Take out the **highest** common factor: $12x - 8 = 4(3x - 2)$, not $2(6x - 4)$, which still shares a 2. A letter can be common too: $2x^2 + 4x = 2x(x + 2)$. Check by expanding: you should get back to where you started. ```

files.working.txt:
# Ava's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: ava
Factorise 12x − 8.
The biggest number that goes into 12 and 8 is 2.
12 ÷ 2 = 6 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
So 12x − 8 = 2(6x − 4).
# endregion
